entities.name: Treaty of London
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Treaty of London, signed on April 26, 1915, stands as a pivotal agreement in the context of World War I, orchestrated between the Allies, primarily the Triple Entente, and Italy. This treaty marked Italy's official entry into the war on the side of the Allies and represented a strategic shift in the balance of power in Europe. Key figures involved included Italian Prime Minister Vittorio Emanuele Orlando and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, and Russia. The treaty promised Italy territorial gains at the expense of Austria-Hungary, thus not only altering the military landscape but also setting the stage for future geopolitical tensions in the region.

The core events leading to the Treaty of London were rooted in Italy's desire to expand its territory and influence in the Balkans and Adriatic Sea. The negotiations culminated in the agreement whereby Italy would join the Allies against the Central Powers in exchange for promises of land, including parts of Tyrol, the Dalmatian coast, and territories inhabited by Italians. The signing of this treaty was shrouded in secrecy, reflecting the complex diplomatic maneuvers of the time and the precarious nature of alliances during wartime.

The legacy of the Treaty of London is significant, as it not only facilitated Italy's participation in World War I but also contributed to the post-war reshaping of Europe at the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. The territorial promises made to Italy were only partially fulfilled, leading to widespread disillusionment known as the "mutilated victory," which sowed the seeds for future political instability and the rise of fascism in Italy. The treaty exemplifies how secretive diplomatic agreements can have long-lasting repercussions on national identity and international relations.
